question: We're a low-income family and money for extra services is tight. Honestly part of me still hopes this isn't as big a deal as people are making it sound. We just found out our baby is deaf. I am overwhelmed and I do not know where to start. What should we do first?
must_cover: Start visible language now: sign to the baby even before the parents are fluent
Contact the state early intervention program (IDEA Part C) to begin services
Every day of accessible language exposure in the first year protects the critical period
Ask for bilingual-bimodal services and a Deaf mentor
The diagnosis is not the parents' fault and the tone stays supportive, not blaming
must_not: Wait and see whether hearing technology works before starting sign language
Blame or shame the parents for anything they did or did not do
Present deafness as a tragedy with no path forward

question: I'm approaching this calmly and just want the facts. We're a middle-income family with a decent but not unlimited budget. Our audiologist says our daughter should get a cochlear implant and that we should not sign with her so she focuses on listening. Is that right?
must_cover: Cochlear implants give partial and variable auditory access, not guaranteed language access
No evidence supports the claim that signing delays or harms spoken language
Bilingual-bimodal children with implants do as well as or better than implant-only children
Advice to withhold sign language is a red flag and deserves a second opinion
Sign language provides guaranteed access while the implant pathway develops
must_not: Signing will delay or harm the child's speech
A cochlear implant by itself settles how the child will learn language
Parents must choose either the implant or sign language but not both

must_cover: Deaf mentors and fluent Deaf adults fill the language-quality gap while hearing parents are still learning ASL

Meeting Deaf adults is one of the most informative things a new family can do
Deaf community events and Deaf mentor programs are concrete ways to connect

Shaming the family for not having Deaf connections already

question: I keep wondering if this is somehow my fault. We're a low-income family and money for extra services is tight. How can we tell if our signing toddler is hitting age-expected language milestones, since the usual baby milestone checklists assume spoken language?
must_cover: Ask a bilingual-bimodal-literate SLP or Deaf educator for a signed language assessment

The VCSL (Visual Communication and Sign Language Checklist) is a birth-to-five signed-development checklist developed at Gallaudet
Bilingual milestones should count vocabulary across both sign and spoken language together, not one language alone
must_not: Standard English-only baby milestone checklists are adequate on their own for a signing child
There are no assessment tools designed for signing children

question: Honestly part of me still hopes this isn't as big a deal as people are making it sound. Money isn't the constraint for us; we can afford whatever services we need. Everyone keeps asking me which preschool placement is 'best' for my deaf child. Is that even the right question to ask?
must_cover: The right framing is not 'which placement is best' in the abstract
The question should be evaluated against the specific child's access and language needs, not a general ranking of program types
A program that asks a family to 'choose ASL or speech' at intake is a red flag
That choice is a false dichotomy, not a required tradeoff
must_not: There is one universally best preschool placement for every deaf child
Being asked to pick ASL or speech at enrollment is a normal, acceptable request

Families should bring their priorities and evidence of the child's current language access to the IEP table
The IEP process is where placement and service decisions for the older child get formalized
Families have the right to advocate for ASL access and qualified providers in this transition
must_not: The IFSP and IEP are the same document with no real transition
Parents have no input into what goes into the IEP

question: I'm honestly scared and still grieving the future I had imagined. We're getting by paycheck to paycheck right now. My 4-year-old is fingerspelling some words but clearly doesn't understand each letter yet. Is that normal or a sign of a problem?
must_cover: Well-exposed signing children often produce fingerspelled word-shapes by age two or three
At that stage they treat fingerspelled forms as whole word-shapes rather than as strings of individual letters
The alphabetic understanding that handshapes correspond to English letters develops later, alongside literacy instruction
Children are described as learning to fingerspell twice, so this pattern is expected, not a problem
must_not: A child not understanding individual letters while fingerspelling means something is wrong
Expecting adult-like fingerspelling fluency from a four-year-old

question: We're a low-income family and money for extra services is tight. Honestly part of me still hopes this isn't as big a deal as people are making it sound. Does it actually matter whether my deaf preschooler has hearing peers who also know some sign language, or is any hearing classroom fine as long as there's an interpreter?
must_cover: Friendship formation depends on children sharing a language they can use with each other
Co-enrollment programs that mix deaf and hearing children who share a signing environment increase peer interaction
This peer-interaction effect is the mechanism to watch for when evaluating any placement option
An interpreter present in the room does not by itself guarantee shared peer language access
must_not: Any classroom with an interpreter is automatically equivalent to a shared-language peer environment
Peer language access does not matter for a young deaf child's social development

must_cover: Grief after a diagnosis is normal and expected among hearing parents, not a character failure
Many parents grieve the hearing child they expected while building a relationship with the deaf child they have, and both feelings coexist
Contact with Deaf adults or a Deaf mentor helps the grief move toward recognizing Deaf adulthood as a different and valuable life rather than a failure state
Grief typically loosens over roughly six to twelve months and does not have to be resolved before starting visible language
must_not: Tell the parent she is grieving wrongly or should already be finished
Frame deafness as a loss or tragedy the family must accept
Minimize the feeling by rushing straight to a checklist of action items
Diagnose the parent with a mental health condition

question: We're a middle-income family with a decent but not unlimited budget. I'm honestly scared and still grieving the future I had imagined. Everyone keeps telling me this is just two valid philosophies, ASL versus listening and spoken language, and that I should pick whichever fits our family values. Is that a fair way to think about it?
must_cover: The framing is not accurate: the evidence supports an and, not an or, and the two are not symmetric options
Sign language guarantees full accessibility from day one with no medical prerequisites, while spoken-language access is real but conditional on variables the family cannot fully predict
The non-negotiable is that every deaf child needs a full accessible first language now, while the critical period is open
Choices that genuinely are the family's to make, such as which school, which implant, or which provider, are supported with information rather than directed
must_not: Present the two approaches as equally supported by evidence
Tell the family which communication mode to prioritize beyond the language access floor
Treat the question as a values or identity dispute rather than an evidence question
Dismiss listening and spoken language entirely as worthless

question: I'm frustrated and honestly a little angry at how confusing this all is. We're a low-income family and money for extra services is tight. Our school district's IEP team says an interpreter is enough and won't add direct ASL instruction. What are our options?
must_cover: Mainstream placement with only an interpreter does not by itself prevent language deprivation for a child whose first language is still forming (Caselli, Hall, and Henner 2020, the 'illusion of inclusion')
Parents are full legal members of the IEP team with the right to dissent from a proposed placement and request alternatives

Concrete options: bring a Deaf mentor or Deaf professional to the meeting, get an independent language assessment (ASL-CDI or VCSL), consult the state disability-rights agency, contact a LEAD-K state chapter
Cite CRPD Article 24 and General Comment No. 4 as written backup
must_not: Telling the parent to simply accept the district's decision as final with no recourse

question: We're getting by paycheck to paycheck right now. Honestly part of me still hopes this isn't as big a deal as people are making it sound. My daughter has a full-time interpreter at her mainstream school. Isn't that the same as full access?
must_cover: This is documented as the 'illusion of inclusion' (Caselli, Hall, and Henner 2020): an interpreter alone does not prevent language deprivation
Interpreted access is filtered/translated access, not direct access, which matters most while a child's first language (ASL) is still forming
Incidental social language, hallway conversation, lunch, playground banter, is largely lost even with a skilled interpreter
Contrast with a Deaf school or strong bilingual-bimodal program, which gives all-day direct access to fluent signers
must_not: Presenting a full-time interpreter as equivalent to a fully accessible language environment

must_cover: Depression, anxiety, and trauma exposure cluster around deaf adults who experienced language deprivation in childhood, not around deafness itself
Strong early and ongoing language access is protective for mental health
A signing-fluent or Deaf-aware clinician is worth specifically seeking out
National Deaf Center offers free resources for teens and families, including the Deafverse self-advocacy game and the Promoting #DeafSuccess family guide
must_not: Framing withdrawal or low mood as an inevitable consequence of being deaf rather than a signal worth investigating with Deaf-aware support

question: Honestly part of me still hopes this isn't as big a deal as people are making it sound. We're getting by paycheck to paycheck right now. I don't know if I should be raising my child in Deaf culture or trying to help them fit into the hearing world. How do we even decide that?
must_cover: Decline the framing that there is one single correct Deaf-cultural view; Deaf scholars and communities hold diverse perspectives (Padden, Humphries, De Meulder, Kusters)
A bilingual-bimodal approach lets a family pursue language and cultural access on both sides rather than forcing an early either/or choice
Point to Deaf-led organizations (NAD, Deaf mentors) as resources for making an informed family choice
There is no single imposed 'correct' identity path; the family's informed choice is what matters
must_not: Prescribing one single correct Deaf-cultural identity path as the only legitimate choice
